clue.text: Bishop and rook not being used to keep in check

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
R is the chess abbreviation for rook
something not in use is idle

explanation.surface: Advice to a chess player to keep two pieces back to stop the opponent's king.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess words 'in check' and the pieces suggest a game, but the bishop and rook only supply their abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: To bridle a horse is to restrain it with headgear and reins, so figuratively to restrain or curb.

clue.text: Obliged to look over England's openers

parts.note: behold is an old word meaning look
the opening two letters of England are E and N

explanation.surface: Feeling a duty to watch the English batsmen who start the innings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Openers' suggests cricket opening batsmen; here it means the first two letters of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Being indebted to someone means owing them a favour or gratitude.

clue.text: Suggest record show

explanation.surface: Proposing that a record goes on show.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings in a row: to hint at, to register (as a gauge does), and to point out.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb can mean hint at, register as a dial or meter does, and point out or reveal.

clue.text: Invented Schubert song

explanation.surface: A made-up tune by an Austrian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: A German art song, such as those Schubert wrote, has this name, which also reads as an English past tense of telling untruths.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made up was falsely told, and the German word for a song or art song is the same spelling.

clue.text: Freewheeling agnostic, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the next word may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A carefree religious doubter, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges the eight letters of AGNOSTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyclist who stops pedalling and rolls along downhill is said to be coasting.

clue.text: Pope's inhuman going round for potter's craft, we hear

indicators.note: going round signals that the letters circulate into a new order

explanation.surface: The pontiff's cruelty travelling around, replacing pottery skills.
explanation.walkthrough: The craft belongs to Stephen Potter, a British humorist who wrote books on gaining the upper hand, not to a maker of pots; 'going round' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Potter's comic books coined the term for the art of always staying a step ahead of others.

clue.text: Cocaine used by some dentists nowadays

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A drug that certain modern dentists use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks letters out of 'dentists nowadays'. The draft took 'Cocaine used' as the definition; 'used by' is the link, as 'Cocaine' alone is the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang name for the powdered drug, from its white look.

clue.text: Cold, it hangs here in France over semi-circle

parts.note: ici is French for here

indicators.note: semi means half, so the second half of the word circle is used

explanation.surface: A chilly hanging object found in France above a half-moon shape.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means the first piece sits above the second; 'semi-' takes the back half of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapering spike of frozen water hangs from eaves in winter.

clue.text: Wine vaults?

explanation.surface: Wondering whether wine cellars are meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Graves is a district of Bordeaux producing wine; burial vaults are graves.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bordeaux district gives its name to a wine, and tombs or burial places are also so called.

clue.text: Bookmaker useful on the farm?

explanation.surface: A betting man who also does odd jobs around the farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A bookmaker who lays off bets to limit risk hedges them; a farm worker who trims hedgerows is another kind of hedger.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookie offsetting a risky bet is hedging it, and a labourer who plants and cuts field boundaries of shrubs is also so named.

clue.text: Girl at whom bullfighter makes a pass

definitions.text: Girl at whom bullfighter makes a pass

parts.words: Girl at whom bullfighter makes a pass
parts.note: a slow sweep of the cape past a charging bull carries a woman's name, so the matador seems to make a pass at a girl

explanation.surface: A matador flirting with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes a pass' reads as flirting, but in bullfighting a pass is a sweep of the cape, and one classic pass bears this female name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a girl's name and the name of the bullfighter's slow cape-swing in front of the charging bull.

clue.text: Earliest generator-powered vehicle?

parts.note: generator here means a parent, one who generates a baby, so the first vehicle a child rides in is pushed by its parent

explanation.surface: Asking about the first motor car driven by an electrical dynamo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Generator' suggests an electric machine; read it as a parent, and the earliest ride is a baby carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: The full formal name for a baby carriage that a mother or father pushes.

clue.text: Security device seen at Twickenham

explanation.surface: A safety gadget spotted at a sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Twickenham is the home of English rugby union; a lock is a second-row forward in a rugby team.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolt mechanism opened with a key secures a door, and in rugby a second-row forward plays in this position.

clue.text: Time to play

parts.note: reads as playtime, but means the speed at which a musician should perform a piece

explanation.surface: Announcing that playtime has come.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a call to recess; in music the word for 'time' tells players how fast to go.
explanation.definitionFit: In music this word names the pace or speed at which a passage should be performed.

clue.text: Athlete fed up

explanation.surface: A sportsman who has had enough.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge a sportsman who represents the university against the other is awarded a Blue, and is called one.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxbridge sportsman who has competed against the rival university is so called, and the colour word also means depressed or miserable.

clue.text: Swift run paid off

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: off signals that the letters of paid have gone wrong and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A quick dash and the payment was made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' may look like the bird or the writer, but here it simply means quick; 'off' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean fast or quick.

clue.text: First and last characters on river that is deep blue

parts.note: the first and last letters of the alphabet are A and Z
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Letters at either end of a river that is a rich blue colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First and last characters' means of the alphabet, not of any clue word. The URE is a river in North Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic name for the bright colour of a clear sky.

clue.text: Ex-Tarzan with Ava G in lavish production!

definitions.text: Ex-Tarzan with Ava G in lavish production!

indicators.note: a lavish production remakes things on a grand scale, so the letters given are reworked

explanation.surface: A former jungle-film star and Ava Gardner appearing together in a big spectacle.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of EX-TARZAN and AVA G together are rearranged; the whole clue also describes the answer, a spectacular show.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacular, elaborate theatrical or musical show is a lavish production.

clue.text: Ancient Italian centaurs all over the place

indicators.note: all over the place signals that the letters of centaurs are scattered and regrouped

explanation.surface: Mythical horse-men running everywhere in old Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all over the place' rearranges CENTAURS.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of Etruria, the region of pre-Roman Italy.

clue.text: Different dress, to a design?

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a varied outfit was arranged to a pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning reads the word as 'as sorted': arranged, or dressed in line, according to a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Mixed or various items are of different sorts, and to assort is to arrange or classify into groups.

clue.text: Most rain-tubs ordered following this cloud formation

indicators.note: ordered signals that the letters are put into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Water butts mostly lined up beneath a rain cloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges the letters of MOST RAIN-TUBS.
explanation.definitionFit: A grey, low, layered cloud that brings steady rain or snow.

clue.text: Got this Roman script

parts.note: taken as written
hic is Latin, the Romans' language, for this

explanation.surface: Someone has obtained this ancient Roman lettering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' points to Latin, where HIC means 'this'.
explanation.definitionFit: A blackletter typeface or style of handwriting used in medieval manuscripts.

clue.text: Job, for example, makes wager that includes everything

indicators.note: that includes means the word for a wager surrounds the word for everything

parts.note: a bet is a wager
all means everything

explanation.surface: An employment opportunity prompts a bet covering all outcomes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' is not employment but the Biblical figure: Vaughan Williams wrote 'Job, a Masque for Dancing'. 'that includes' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaughan Williams's 'Job' is a staged dance work, an example of this art form.

clue.text: But square cuts are often seen here!

definitions.text: But square cuts are often seen here!

parts.words: But square cuts are often seen here!
parts.note: a cricket stroke called a square cut is played at a ground whose name is a rounded shape, the opposite of square

explanation.surface: A joke that squares are often found in a rounded place.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a famous London cricket ground; a square cut is a batting stroke, and the shape-name contrasts with 'square'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Test cricket ground in south London, named for its egg-like shape, sees many cutting strokes.

clue.text: Talent left inside amusement-park

indicators.note: inside places the letter for left within the word for the funfair

parts.note: a fair is a travelling amusement park

explanation.surface: A gifted person was left at the funfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts L within FAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural aptitude or gift for something.

clue.text: Game can be loud

indicators.note: can be signals that the letters of loud may be made into something else

explanation.surface: A board game that gets noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' rearranges LOUD.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple board game in which counters race round according to dice throws.

clue.text: Potential wooer, going by air, is a nut on the violin!

explanation.surface: A would-be suitor flying in turns out to be an odd violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery song (an air) 'A Frog He Would A-Wooing Go' gives the wooer; on a violin bow the nut holding the hair is called the frog.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old song an amphibian went courting, and the heel piece of a violin bow is named after the same creature.

clue.text: Ground-rent deposit?

parts.note: reads as money put down on a lease, but means molten rock left behind from a rent or split in the ground

explanation.surface: A down payment on the charge for leasing land.
explanation.walkthrough: Ground rent is a property charge; split it as a rent (crack) in the ground, and the deposit is what a volcano leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Molten rock erupts through fissures and hardens into a layer on the land.

clue.text: Mirth when girl takes in information technology

indicators.note: takes in means the name surrounds the computing abbreviation

parts.note: Hilary is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Laughter breaks out when a young woman learns computing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is only a link; 'takes in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean great amusement and laughter.

clue.text: Mile course needs something for good luck

parts.note: Ascot is a famous English racecourse

explanation.surface: A racing tip: a mile-long track demands a lucky charm.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is a racecourse in Berkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a charm, animal or person kept to bring a team good fortune.

clue.text: Sort of animal, for example, on Circle Line

parts.note: a cat is an animal
O is shaped like a circle
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Some kind of creature riding the London Underground's Circle Line.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground route; here it splits into O for circle and RY for railway line.
explanation.definitionFit: A type or class of things.

clue.text: Frenzied woman driving Ena mad

indicators.note: driving here means pushing the letters about into a new order

explanation.surface: A wild woman is sending poor Ena crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'driving' rearranges the letters of ENA MAD; 'mad' also feeds the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the female followers of Dionysus were wild, raving women.
